expectedText:
REPORTING TIME PAY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

POLICY STATEMENT
Acme Corp maintains this Reporting Time Pay Information Sheet to describe the reporting-time-pay requirements that apply to non-exempt employees, including Jordan Alex Lee, under the applicable California IWC Wage Order. Acme Corp states its intention to comply with those requirements as they apply to a scheduled reporting, a second reporting in the same workday, and the related split-shift premium described in this document. This policy is a statement of Acme Corp's practice; it does not itself expand, limit, or waive any right or obligation that may exist under applicable law.

REPORTING TIME PAY — THE CORE RULE
California law requires Acme Corp to pay Jordan Alex Lee for each workday that Jordan Alex Lee is required to report for work and does report, but is not put to work or is furnished less than half of Jordan Alex Lee's usual or scheduled day's work. The required payment is half of Jordan Alex Lee's usual or scheduled day's work, but in no event less than two hours nor more than four hours, at Jordan Alex Lee's regular rate of pay, which may not be less than the applicable minimum wage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Each workday an employee is required to report for work and does report, but is not put to work or is furnished less than half said employee’s usual or scheduled day’s work, the employee shall be paid for half the usual or scheduled day’s work, but in no event for less than two (2) hours nor more than four (4) hours, at the employee’s regular rate of pay, which shall not be less than the minimum wage."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This provision does not appear in the California Labor Code — it is a regulation adopted by the Industrial Welfare Commission, codified in IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), the general catch-all order used elsewhere in this corpus (see the rest-period and meal-period clauses) because it applies broadly rather than to one industry. Other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for public housekeeping or Wage Order 7 for mercantile employees) contain reporting-time-pay language in the same numbered section with materially the same formula, but those other orders were not independently fetched or checked in this session — this clause verifies Wage Order 4-2001 only. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law (the Fair Labor Standards Act) has no reporting-time-pay requirement at all, and most states impose none either; California's rule is unusually protective by national comparison. This is a single regulatory subdivision (§ 5(A)); no additional independent source was located for this specific formula. This clause states a fact about what the law requires — it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how that formula applies to a particular workday, schedule, or pay period.

REPORTING TIME PAY FOR A SECOND REPORTING IN THE SAME WORKDAY
Separately from the core reporting-time-pay rule, if Jordan Alex Lee is required to report for work a second time in the same workday and is furnished less than two hours of work on that second reporting, California law requires Acme Corp to pay Jordan Alex Lee for two hours at Jordan Alex Lee's regular rate of pay, which may not be less than the applicable minimum wage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If an employee is required to report for work a second time in any one workday and is furnished less than two (2) hours of work on the second reporting, said employee shall be paid for two (2) hours at the employee’s regular rate of pay, which shall not be less than the minimum wage."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(B), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(B) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is a separate, second-reporting rule within the same regulatory section as the core reporting-time-pay rule (§ 5(A)) — both are subdivisions of IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5, so this clause and the core-rule clause elsewhere in this document draw on the same source, not independent corroboration of each other. Unlike the first-reporting formula in § 5(A), which pays half the scheduled day (bounded between two and four hours), this second-reporting rule sets a flat two-hour minimum with no formula tied to the scheduled day's length and no four-hour cap stated in this subdivision. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law has no comparable requirement, and most states impose none either. This clause states a fact about what the law requires; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how it applies to a particular workday.

EXCEPTIONS TO REPORTING TIME PAY
California's reporting-time-pay requirements do not apply when operations cannot commence or continue because of a threat to employees or property, or because civil authorities recommend that work not begin; when public utilities fail to supply electricity, water, or gas, or there is a failure in the public utilities or sewer system; or when the interruption of work is caused by an act of God or another cause outside Acme Corp's control. Separately, the reporting-time-pay requirements do not apply to Jordan Alex Lee while on paid standby status who is called in to perform assigned work at a time other than Jordan Alex Lee's scheduled reporting time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The foregoing reporting time pay provisions are not applicable when: (1) Operations cannot commence or continue due to threats to employees or property; or when recommended by civil authorities; or (2) Public utilities fail to supply electricity, water, or gas, or there is a failure in the public utilities, or sewer system; or (3) The interruption of work is caused by an Act of God or other cause not within the employer’s control."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(C), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(C)(1)-(3) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "This section shall not apply to an employee on paid standby status who is called to perform assigned work at a time other than the employee’s scheduled reporting time."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(D), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(D) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: The two citations below, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(C) and § 5(D), are both subdivisions of the same regulatory section (§ 5) as the core reporting-time-pay rule and the second-reporting rule cited elsewhere in this document — they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. Subdivision (C) lists three circumstances under which the reporting-time-pay obligations described elsewhere in this document do not apply; subdivision (D) is a separate, narrower carve-out limited to employees on paid standby status who are called in outside their scheduled reporting time — the wage order's own text does not list it as a fourth item within subdivision (C)'s list, though it has the same practical effect of taking a situation outside the reporting-time-pay requirement. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law has no comparable requirement or exceptions to it. This clause states facts about what the law provides; it does not determine whether any specific employer's operational shutdown, utility failure, or standby arrangement actually satisfies these provisions.

REPORTING TIME PAY REQUIRES ACTUAL REPORTING
California's reporting-time-pay rule, by its own terms, applies when an employee 'is required to report for work and does report.' The wage order's text does not address, in these words, what happens when Acme Corp notifies Jordan Alex Lee that a shift is cancelled before Jordan Alex Lee reports for that shift — whether reporting-time pay is owed in that circumstance is a fact-specific question this text alone does not resolve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "is required to report for work and does report"
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause's citation is the same wage order subdivision quoted in the core-rule clause elsewhere in this document (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A)) — not an independent source, but the same text examined for a different interpretive point: the rule is triggered only when the employee 'is required to report for work and does report.' The wage order's text does not, in these words, address what happens when an employer cancels or changes a shift before the employee reports — for example, by notifying the employee the night before that a shift is cancelled. This clause does not assert a definitive answer to that scenario; it states only what the quoted text itself says (that actual reporting is a stated element of the rule) and flags the pre-report-cancellation question as genuinely unresolved by the text quoted here. Practitioner or agency guidance addressing advance-notice cancellations was not independently verified in this session and is not relied on. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause states a fact about what the text says and does not say; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how to handle a particular scheduling change.

REPORTING TIME PAY IS SEPARATE FROM OVERTIME AND MEAL/REST PREMIUM PAY
Reporting time pay is a separate wage requirement from California's overtime rules and from the premium pay owed for a missed meal or rest period. Nothing in the reporting-time-pay provisions reduces, replaces, or is satisfied by wages Acme Corp owes Jordan Alex Lee under those other requirements, and nothing in those other requirements reduces or satisfies the reporting-time-pay obligation described in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the employee shall be paid for half the usual or scheduled day’s work, but in no event for less than two (2) hours nor more than four (4) hours, at the employee’s regular rate of pay, which shall not be less than the minimum wage"
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause cites the same wage order subdivision as the core-rule clause elsewhere in this document (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A)) — not an independent source for this specific point, but the operative text establishing that reporting time pay is itself a wage payment computed under its own formula. The wage order does not, in these words, state expressly that reporting time pay is "in addition to" or "not an offset against" other wage requirements; that conclusion is drawn here from the fact that overtime (governed by this same wage order's Section 3, not independently re-verified in this session) and meal/rest period premium pay (governed by California Labor Code § 226.7, already verified in this corpus's meal-and-rest-break-policy document as the clause mealrest_premium_pay) are stated in separate, independently numbered provisions with their own triggering conditions and formulas, none of which cross-references or reduces the Section 5 reporting-time-pay obligation. This document does not restate the overtime or meal/rest premium rules; readers are directed to this corpus's existing overtime and meal-and-rest-break-policy clauses for those requirements. This is one state's regulatory framework, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause states a fact about how these requirements relate structurally; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how to calculate total wages owed for a particular pay period.

THE SPLIT SHIFT PREMIUM (A RELATED, SEPARATE REQUIREMENT)
Related to, but distinct from, reporting time pay, California law requires Acme Corp to pay Jordan Alex Lee one additional hour of pay at the minimum wage for any workday Jordan Alex Lee works a split shift — a schedule interrupted by an unpaid, non-working period other than a bona fide meal or rest period — except when Jordan Alex Lee resides at the place of employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "When an employee works a split shift, one (1) hour’s pay at the minimum wage shall be paid in addition to the minimum wage for that workday, except when the employee resides at the place of employment."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(C), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 4(C) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is a related but conceptually distinct wage requirement, found in the same wage order's minimum-wage section rather than its reporting-time-pay section: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(C). A split shift triggers its own one-hour premium at minimum wage, separate from, and calculated differently than, the reporting-time-pay formulas described elsewhere in this document — the split-shift premium does not depend on whether the employee was sent home early or given a second reporting event, and the reporting-time-pay rules do not depend on whether the day's schedule was split. This clause was verified from the same primary-source PDF fetched for the reporting-time-pay clauses in this document, but § 4(C) is a single regulatory subdivision; no additional independent source was located for the split-shift premium formula. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law has no comparable split-shift premium. This clause states a fact about what the law requires; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how it applies to a particular schedule.

SIGNATURE AND RECEIPT
